title: Sliding Window (Variable Size): Longest Substring Without Repeats
oneLiner: Grow the window on the right; when it breaks the rule, shrink it from the left until it's valid again.
keyTakeaway: A variable-size window keeps one invariant -- here, "no character appears twice". Extend right by one each step; while the invariant is broken, move left forward. Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so the whole scan is O(n) even though there's a loop inside a loop.
explanation:
The fixed-size sliding window lesson moved a window of exactly k elements. Many real problems don't give you k: they give you a rule the window must satisfy and ask for the longest (or shortest) window that does. Longest substring with no repeated character is the classic one: in "abcabcbb" the answer is 3 ("abc").

Keep two indices, left and right, and a set (or count map) of the characters currently in the window. Each step, move right forward and look at the new character. If it's already in the window, the rule is broken, so remove characters from the left end (and move left forward) until the duplicate is gone. Then add the new character and record the window size, right - left + 1, if it's the best so far.

It looks quadratic -- there's a while loop inside the for loop -- but left only ever moves forward, so across the whole run it moves at most n times. Every character is added once and removed at most once: O(n). (A refinement stores each character's last index in a map and jumps left straight past it instead of stepping.)

The same grow-then-shrink loop solves "smallest subarray with sum ≥ target", "longest substring with at most k distinct characters" and many more -- only the rule and what you track change.

recognitionSignals: Longest or shortest CONTIGUOUS substring/subarray that satisfies a condition (no repeats, at most k distinct, sum at least X).
No fixed window size is given -- the condition decides how big the window can be.
Once a window breaks the rule, any larger window containing it also breaks it, so shrinking from the left is safe.
gotchas: Shrink with a WHILE loop, not an if -- the duplicate may be several characters back from left.
Remove the left character from the set before moving left forward, or the set and the window drift apart.
Measure the window AFTER restoring the rule, not before; size is right - left + 1.
confusableWith: Sliding Window: Max Sum Subarray of Size K (this track) is the fixed-size version: both ends move together every step. Here the right end always advances but the left end only moves when the rule breaks.
Two Pointers (this track): both use two indices, but two pointers usually start at opposite ends and close in; window pointers both move left to right.

complexity.note: right visits each index once and left only moves forward, so each character enters and leaves the window at most once. The set holds at most k distinct characters (the alphabet size), and never more than n.

referenceSolutions.python:
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    window = set()
    left = best = 0
    for right, c in enumerate(s):
        while c in window:  # shrink until the repeat is gone
            window.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        window.add(c)
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
